title: RL Terms for LLMs: How One Score Reaches Every Token

images.caption: DeepSeek-R1-Zero: a rule checks only the final answer, yet AIME 2024 pass@1 rose from 15.6% to 71.0% during RL (published). The token grid is schematic.
images.target_after_text: In January 2025, DeepSeek reported DeepSeek-R1-Zero, a model trained with reinforcement learning (RL) directly on a bas...
images.target_after_text_full: In January 2025, DeepSeek reported DeepSeek-R1-Zero, a model trained with reinforcement learning (RL) directly on a base model, without supervised fine-tuning first. Its reward came from rules: one rule checks whether the final answer is correct, another checks that the reasoning is placed between think tags. Over thousands of RL steps, its pass@1 on the AIME 2024 math competition rose from 15.6% to 71.0%, and to 86.7% with majority voting. Its responses also grew longer during training: the model learned to spend more tokens on reasoning.

images.target_block_html: In January 2025, DeepSeek reported DeepSeek-R1-Zero, a model trained with reinforcement learning (RL) directly on a base model, without supervised fine-tuning first. Its reward came from rules: one rule checks whether the final answer is correct, another checks that the reasoning is placed between think tags. Over thousands of RL steps, its pass@1 on the AIME 2024 math competition rose from 15.6% to 71.0%, and to 86.7% with majority voting. Its responses also grew longer during training: the model learned to spend more tokens on reasoning.

images.caption: Ten sampled answers land at their scores. All ten averaged give V = 4.3, each branch's average is its Q (2, 5, 9), and A = Q − V is −2.3, +0.7, +4.7. Illustrative numbers.
images.target_after_text: The advantage A(s, a) = Q(s, a) − V(s) is the average score after writing token a in state s, minus the average with no...
images.target_after_text_full: The advantage A(s, a) = Q(s, a) − V(s) is the average score after writing token a in state s, minus the average with no token fixed: how much better or worse writing a is than what the model usually does. For example, A(open) = Q(open) − V = 2 − 4.3 = −2.3: answers that start with open score 2.3 below the average. Likewise A(closed) = 5 − 4.3 = +0.7 and A(partly) = 9 − 4.3 = +4.7.
images.next_text: The figure puts the three in one picture. Ten sampled answers land at their own scores. The dots of one branch fall to...
images.next_text_full: The figure puts the three in one picture. Ten sampled answers land at their own scores. The dots of one branch fall to their average, which is that branch's Q, and all ten averaged give V. The state sits at the height of V = 4.3, and the arrow from the V line to each Q is the advantage.
images.target_block_html: • The advantage A(s, a) = Q(s, a) − V(s) is the average score after writing token a in state s, minus the average with no token fixed: how much better or worse writing a is than what the model usually does. For example, A(open) = Q(open) − V = 2 − 4.3 = −2.3: answers that start with open score 2.3 below the average. Likewise A(closed) = 5 − 4.3 = +0.7 and A(partly) = 9 − 4.3 = +4.7.

images.caption: V drops right after open, so the TD error of −2.3 puts the blame there. λ = 0 keeps it on open; λ = 1 spreads it to OpenAI and is.
images.target_after_text: Credit goes to the token where the expected score changed.
images.target_after_text_full: Credit goes to the token where the expected score changed.
images.next_text: This depends on an accurate V, and in practice V is a learned estimate. GAE (generalized advantage estimation) adds a d...
images.next_text_full: This depends on an accurate V, and in practice V is a learned estimate. GAE (generalized advantage estimation) adds a dial, λ, between 0 and 1. With λ = 0, each token's advantage is its own TD error, and the blame stays on open. With λ = 1, each token's advantage is the final score minus V at that token, so OpenAI, is and open all get −2.3. That spreads blame onto tokens that did nothing wrong, since every answer starts with OpenAI is; over many samples this noise averages out. λ = 0 trusts V, λ = 1 trusts only the final score, and PPO commonly uses a value near 0.95.
images.target_block_html: Credit goes to the token where the expected score changed.

images.caption: Two policy-gradient steps: the branches reshape (50/30/20% → 15/36/49% → 4/11/85%) and V rises from 4.3 to 8.3; closed turns from above to below average. Illustrative step size.
images.target_after_text: With an advantage for every token, the update can be stated in one line: raise the log-probability of tokens with A abo...
images.target_after_text_full: With an advantage for every token, the update can be stated in one line: raise the log-probability of tokens with A above 0 and lower it for tokens with A below 0, in proportion to A. This is the policy gradient. At our state, it moves each next-token logit by an amount proportional to π × A.
images.next_text: Two exact update steps, with an illustrative step size, take the probabilities from 0.50 / 0.30 / 0.20 to 0.15 / 0.36 /...
images.next_text_full: Two exact update steps, with an illustrative step size, take the probabilities from 0.50 / 0.30 / 0.20 to 0.15 / 0.36 / 0.49, then to 0.04 / 0.11 / 0.86. V rises from 4.3 to 6.5 to 8.3. In the first step closed rises, since 5 beats 4.3. Once V passes 5, closed is below average and falls. The advantage is measured against the current model, so the bar keeps rising as the model improves.
images.target_block_html: With an advantage for every token, the update can be stated in one line: raise the log-probability of tokens with A above 0 and lower it for tokens with A below 0, in proportion to A. This is the policy gradient. At our state, it moves each next-token logit by an amount proportional to π × A.

images.caption: Greedy decoding only takes open: the other branches stay unknown, A = 0, and nothing changes. Sampling tries every branch and the policy moves.

images.target_after_text_full: Sampling at temperature 1 sometimes writes closed or partly. Those samples show that the other branches score higher, and they are what move the policy. This is exploration: the policy has to try less likely tokens, so RL training samples its answers.

images.caption: The batch was sampled from π_old. A = +4.7 pushes π(partly) from 20% to 24%; ρ = π / π_old reaches 1 + ε (ε = 0.2) and the push stops.
images.target_after_text: Ratio and clipping. The policy gradient assumes the answers came from the current policy, which is called on-policy dat...
images.target_after_text_full: Ratio and clipping. The policy gradient assumes the answers came from the current policy, which is called on-policy data. Sampling is expensive, so PPO-style training samples a batch with the current model, keeps a frozen copy π_old, and takes several update steps on that batch. After a few steps the model π has moved away from π_old. The importance ratio ρ = π / π_old measures how far, for each sampled token, and reweights its contribution. Clipping stops the update once ρ leaves the window from 1 − ε to 1 + ε. With ε = 0.2 and π_old(partly) = 0.2, the advantage of +4.7 can raise π(partly) to 0.24 on this batch and no further. Further progress needs fresh samples.
images.next_text: KL penalty. A judge is reliable only near the kind of answers it was built on. Suppose the judge likes flattery: it giv...
images.next_text_full: KL penalty. A judge is reliable only near the kind of answers it was built on. Suppose the judge likes flattery: it gives partly. Some open weights. a 9 and partly. What a brilliant question! a 9.6. The reference model π_ref, the SFT model before RL, writes the flattering version 5% of the time. With nothing to stop it, RL would push the policy toward flattery. The KL penalty subtracts β × KL(π‖π_ref) from the reward, where KL measures how far the policy's distribution has moved from the reference. With β = 1, as the policy's share of flattery drifts from 5% to 90%, the judge's average rises only from 9.03 to 9.54, while the KL term reaches 2.38 and R − β × KL falls from 9.03 to 7.16. Drifting toward flattery lowers the objective, so the policy stays near the reference. Real systems compute KL token by token and use a much smaller β; β = 1 here makes the effect visible.
images.target_block_html: Ratio and clipping. The policy gradient assumes the answers came from the current policy, which is called on-policy data. Further progress needs fresh samples.

reverse_images.target_after_text_full: In January 2025, DeepSeek reported DeepSeek-R1-Zero, a model trained with reinforcement learning (RL) directly on a base model, without supervised fine-tuning first. Its reward came from rules: one rule checks whether the final answer is correct, another checks that the reasoning is placed between think tags. Over thousands of RL steps, its pass@1 on the AIME 2024 math competition rose from 15.6% to 71.0%, and to 86.7% with majority voting. Its responses also grew longer during training: the model learned to spend more tokens on reasoning.

reverse_images.target_block_html: In January 2025, DeepSeek reported DeepSeek-R1-Zero, a model trained with reinforcement learning (RL) directly on a base model, without supervised fine-tuning first. Its reward came from rules: one rule checks whether the final answer is correct, another checks that the reasoning is placed between think tags. Over thousands of RL steps, its pass@1 on the AIME 2024 math competition rose from 15.6% to 71.0%, and to 86.7% with majority voting. Its responses also grew longer during training: the model learned to spend more tokens on reasoning.
